source: Zhang, Wisniewski, Tomeh, Charnois (2025) Reasoning Strategies in Large Language Models: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: Prompts can steer LLMs into four named reasoning strategies (supposition following, chain construction, compound, concatenation), but no strategy beats the plain prompt with no strategy named.
numbers: TruthQuest (2,400 items) accuracy, Phi-4 / R1-Distill: no strategy 47.2 / 63.4; supposition 45.1 / 62.7; chain 49.0 / 62.5; compound 47.1 / 61.4; concatenation 47.4 / 63.0. ZebraLogic (1,000 puzzles), Phi-4 / Qwen3: no strategy 27.3 / 32.0; other prompts 25.1 to 27.0 / 31.0 to 32.0. Strategy adherence checked by hand on 100 answers per model.
quote: explicitly specifying a strategy in the prompt does not improve problem-solving performance
limits: Two logic benchmarks only, small open models (14B, 8B, distilled). Regex answer check.
agent_relevance: A fixed strategy label in the prompt is not a gain by itself. Strategy routing must earn its keep on measured items (supports G1, 4b).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in LLMs, oracle analysis
finding: An oracle that picks the best strategy per item would add a lot of accuracy, so strategies fail on different items.
numbers: Oracle (any of the 4 strategy prompts correct) TruthQuest 82.9 (Phi-4) and 90.1 (R1-Distill) versus best single 49.0 and 63.4. ZebraLogic oracle 37.7 and 36.4 versus 27.3 and 32.0. Gain up to about 40 points.
limits: The oracle is partly selection from noise: taking the best of 4 samples of a stochastic model raises it even if strategies were identical. The paper has no same-prompt resampling control for this.
agent_relevance: Do not read the oracle gap as proof that strategy choice is learnable. Compare with a resample-only oracle before building a router (G4).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in LLMs, merging and selection
finding: Running all strategies and merging the answers in code beat any single strategy, but stayed far below the oracle; no merge rule won everywhere; the model-based verifier was unstable.
numbers: TruthQuest Phi-4: best single 49.0, majority vote 54.9, vote+prob 57.3, vote+verifier 55.8, verifier alone 46.9, oracle 82.9. R1-Distill: best single 63.4, verifier 74.1, vote+verifier 72.6, majority 68.4. ZebraLogic gains only +0.6 to +1.0 for Phi-4 (majority 27.9 vs 27.3).
limits: Voting over strategies mixes the effect of strategy diversity with the effect of plain sampling. Gains vanish on the harder ZebraLogic.
agent_relevance: Code-side selection works, model-side strategy choice does not. Agrees with G5. Strategy voters add little on hard multi-valued problems.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in LLMs, difficulty analysis
finding: Strategy differences are small and shift with problem size; no strategy is best across sizes.
numbers: TruthQuest Phi-4 by number of persons (3/4/5/6): single strategy accuracy 74.2/69.5/61.0/49.0 percent; supposition best at 3 persons (77.7), compound best at 3 persons (79.3), no strategy best at 4 persons (68.3 vs 66.3). ZebraLogic hard puzzles about 8 percent for all strategies.
limits: Per-cell samples are small, so rank orders between strategies are within noise.
agent_relevance: Difficulty, not strategy name, drives the result. A difficulty signal from code (size, failed checks) is a more promising routing input than a strategy label.

source: Zhou, Zhong, Wang, Wang (2024) Adaptive-Solver Framework for Dynamic Strategy Selection in LLM Reasoning
finding: Start with a cheap solver and switch to a costlier setting (stronger model, more samples, different prompt, finer decomposition) only when answer consistency says the answer is unreliable. This kept GPT-4 level accuracy at lower cost.
numbers: 8 reasoning datasets (e.g. GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, MAWPS, CSQA). Cost down 46 to 85 percent versus always using GPT-4 at comparable accuracy; up to 4.5 points higher accuracy at equal cost. GSM8K 92.49 vs best same-budget baseline 87.93; SVAMP 90.75 vs 88.75. Model switching raised cost 20 to 30 times; prompt-method switching 1 to 2 times.
limits: Needs a training set to pre-build the solver pipeline per dataset; consistency is a weak reliability signal (correlated errors). Math and QA tasks, GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: A signal-triggered escalation ladder matches G1 and the S0 gate. Escalate on disagreement, not on a schedule. Note that consistency is only a hint (G4).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: The model picks and adapts atomic reasoning modules (about 39 seed modules) into a task-level reasoning structure with 3 extra calls, then follows it per instance. Large gains on some tasks, small on others.
numbers: Accuracy BBH / T4D / MATH. PaLM 2-L: direct 56/30/45; CoT 60/40/42; plan-and-solve 61/42/49; Self-Discover 67/69/50.5. GPT-4: direct 58/51/70.5; CoT 75/52/71; plan-and-solve 73/53/70; Self-Discover 81/85/73. Beats CoT on 21 of 25 BBH tasks. 10 to 40 times fewer inference calls than CoT-self-consistency or per-module voting. Structures found by PaLM 2-L transfer to GPT-4; GPT-4 structures help Llama2 (52 vs CoT 42 on disambiguation QA).
limits: Authors' own benchmark choice. MATH gains only 1 to 7 points (PaLM) and 2 to 3 (GPT-4); 74.7 percent of MATH errors are computation errors, only 25.3 percent wrong structure. 87.5 percent of 200 audited structures were correct. Largest gains on algorithmic tasks (T4D).
agent_relevance: Strongest positive evidence for scaffolded strategy selection, yet it works at task level with a few seed modules, and the gain is where the base model lacks a procedure. Fits O1-O8 as a small module menu.

source: Gunasekara, Ratnayake (2025) Effects of structure on reasoning in instance-level Self-Discover
finding: Rival to Self-Discover: when the plan is made per instance, free-text plans beat dynamically generated JSON-structured plans, and task-level plans can beat instance-level ones on coherent tasks.
numbers: LLaMA / Mistral accuracy. MATH (1-shot): structured 63.50 / 67.50; unstructured 75.50 / 76.50 (relative +18.90 and +13.33 percent). BBH avg: Self-Discover baseline 86.59 / 82.04; iSD struct 85.05 / 83.14; unstruct 87.27 / 85.57. T4D: task-level Self-Discover 100.00 / 96.63 vs unstruct 78.90 / 82.09 and struct 73.23 / 76.06. 5-shot guidance helped T4D (+9.44 and +7.55 percent relative) but not BBH.
limits: Two open models only; 'baseline' MATH row is the same run as the structured variant; T4D set is highly homogeneous, favouring task-level plans.
agent_relevance: Rigid JSON strategy structure can hurt. Keep strategy menus short and in free text; share a plan across similar items instead of re-planning each one.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Route to Reason: Adaptive Routing for LLM and Reasoning Strategy Selection
finding: A learned router picks a (model, strategy) pair per query from predicted correctness and predicted token cost, cutting tokens by more than half at equal or better accuracy than the strongest model.
numbers: In-distribution (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-STEM, OlympiadBench): RTR 82.5 percent at 1091 tokens vs QwQ-32B 80.0 at 2745, EmbedLLM 81.9 at 1808, RouteLLM 77.3, KNN 76.9 at 1101, random 69.5. Out-of-distribution (SciQ, PIQA, ARC-C): RTR 94.2 at 394 tokens vs QwQ-32B 93.7 at 1387. Strategies: vanilla, CoT, PAL, Chain-of-Draft. Token predictor within 200 tokens about 80 percent for non-reasoning models, within 600 about 60 percent for reasoning models.
limits: Read from the arXiv HTML page, not the PDF. Subsets of 300 to 600 items per benchmark; the router needs labeled training data; models are small open models; one strategy per query.
agent_relevance: Routing pays off mostly through cost (choosing when not to think long), less through accuracy. Relevant to adaptive stopping; needs data we do not have for a single-model agent.

source: Suzgun, Kalai (2024) Meta-Prompting: Task-Agnostic Scaffolding
finding: One model acts as conductor, splits the task, sends subtasks to fresh instances of itself as 'experts' and checks results.
numbers: GPT-4 average over Game of 24, Checkmate-in-One, Python Programming Puzzles: meta-prompting with Python interpreter beat standard prompting by 17.1 percent, expert prompting by 17.3, multipersona by 15.2 (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the paper. Gains partly come from the code interpreter. Multi-persona style experts conflict with G4.
agent_relevance: Conductor-and-experts is a persona-voter variant; our guardrails forbid persona voters on single-answer problems. Treat gains as unverified for our case.

source: Stadler, Becker, Goedker, Leutner, Greiff (2015) Complex problem solving and intelligence: A meta-analysis
finding: Complex problem solving (CPS) and intelligence overlap clearly but are not the same. How CPS was measured changed the correlation; how intelligence was measured did not.
numbers: 47 studies, 60 independent samples, N = 13,740; mean correlation .433 (as reported by the search summary and by later papers that cite it, including Wu and Molnar 2022). Newest CPS assessment type (MicroDYN style) showed the strongest associations.
limits: Full text was behind a paywall (certificate error); numbers taken from abstract-level summaries only. Strongest links come from the very tests that have the weakest ecological validity (Doerner and Funke critique).
agent_relevance: CPS performance in minimal systems is largely reasoning ability, so strategy gains there may not transfer to open ill-defined problems.

source: Doerner, Funke (2017) Complex Problem Solving: What It Is and What It Is Not
finding: Rival views of CPS. Doerner: self-regulated processes in dynamic, ill-defined, high-stakes settings (Lohhausen, over 2,000 variables, 10 simulated years in about 10 hours). Funke and Greiff: minimal systems such as MicroDYN (3 to 5 variables, about 3 minutes of exploration) can capture CPS. Doerner and Funke now warn that minimal systems risk becoming 'minimal valid systems'.
numbers: Microworld sizes: Tailorshop about 20 variables, Moro about 60, Lohhausen about 2,000. In Lohhausen conventional IQ did not predict performance; calm under challenge and switching between analytic and holistic processing did. Wuestenberg et al. (2012) cited for a small gain over reasoning tests in predicting school grades. Read only the first 100,000 of 146,471 characters.
limits: Conceptual paper, almost no new data; Lohhausen claims rest on a 1980s study with small samples and have been contested elsewhere.
agent_relevance: The well-defined versus ill-defined split is the honest boundary for our scaffold: strategy repertoires are validated on small well-defined systems, not on Lohhausen-like problems.

source: Schoppek, Fischer (2017) Common Process Demands of Two Complex Dynamic Control Tasks: Transfer Is Mediated by Comprehensive Strategies
finding: Practising MicroDYN helped on the real-time task Dynamis2, but not the other way round. The expected mediator, the vary-one-thing-at-a-time strategy (VOTAT), did not carry the transfer; a different strategy, PULSE (set inputs to zero and watch the system run on its own), did.
numbers: N = 165, full crossing of source and target task. MicroDYN-first group beat Dynamis2-first group on Dynamis2: t(81) = 1.82, one-sided p < .05, d = 0.40; estimated transfer about 40 percent (Katona formula). MicroDYN explains a unique 15.4 percent of Dynamis2 variance beyond figural reasoning (beta .402); reasoning adds 7.4 percent; R = .54. VOTAT use difference between groups d = 0.46, but VOTAT-performance correlation in Dynamis2 only r = .28. Overall condition effect F(2,121) = 9.11, partial eta-squared .132.
limits: Transfer test is an exploratory finding (the PULSE explanation was not pre-registered; the authors say so). One direction only; power 0.72 for d = 0.5.
agent_relevance: The textbook strategy (VOTAT) may not be what transfers. Check which behaviour actually carries gains before baking it into an operator.

source: Molnar, Csapo (2018) The Efficacy and Development of Students' Problem-Solving Strategies During Compulsory Schooling: Logfile Analyses
finding: Using the theoretically right strategy does not guarantee success, and a right answer does not prove the right strategy. Conscious VOTAT users did best, then non-conscious VOTAT users, then others.
numbers: N = 4,371 students (grades 3 to 12, Hungary), MicroDYN problems on eDia. Share of effective strategy use and high performance ranged 20 to 80 percent depending on complexity and age. Effective-strategy use rose about 20 percent per age step and fell about 20 percent with more input variables. Pure isolated variation made up 45 percent of VOTAT uses and was the only one that reliably gave the correct solution (about 80 percent correct in the oldest cohort). Guessing (correct answer without an effective strategy) was common: e.g. 71.8 percent high achievement among non-effective users in one grade 3 to 5 cell.
limits: Strategy coding from logfiles only; latent classes depend on coding choices; no experimental manipulation; Hungarian sample.
agent_relevance: Right strategy is neither necessary nor sufficient. This supports G3: judge by a check on the outcome, not by whether the trace looks like the right method.

source: Wu, Molnar (2022) Logfile analyses of exploration strategies in CPS and links to inductive and combinatorial reasoning
finding: Most university students use proper exploration strategies; the few who do not score far lower, and reasoning ability predicts performance within every strategy profile.
numbers: N = 1,343 first-year students, MicroDYN 12 scenarios. Four latent profiles: proficient 84.3 percent (CPS mean 61.37), rapid learners 6.2 (35.39), non-persistent explorers 3.1 (27.03), non-performing explorers 6.5 (22.75). CPS differs by profile F(3,1339) = 187.28, p < .001. Inductive reasoning predicts CPS in all profiles (beta .309 to .432); combinatorial reasoning only in the proficient group (beta .104).
limits: Cross-sectional, single university, voluntary low-stakes sample (43.4 percent took part), well-defined MicroDYN only; the causal reading that reasoning training should come first is not supported by the data (authors' own limit).
agent_relevance: Strategy use and general reasoning are confounded. Do not credit a strategy for what better reasoners do anyway.

source: Editorial (2018) Complex Problem Solving Beyond the Psychometric Approach
finding: Summary of a special issue: effective knowledge-acquisition strategies predict control performance but are neither necessary nor sufficient; Suess and Kretzschmar find little reason to posit a CPS ability beyond knowledge and reasoning; prior knowledge can help or hinder; motivation matters but is hard to prove.
numbers: No new numbers; counts only.
limits: Editorial, not data.
agent_relevance: Incremental validity of a separate CPS skill over reasoning plus knowledge is doubtful, which cuts against building the agent around a general 'CPS skill'.

source: Boom (2015) Overlapping waves as 3D latent growth plus IRT model
finding: A methods paper to make Siegler's overlapping-waves idea testable: strategies lie on one ordered dimension, and a latent growth curve moves a child along it. Waves could arise from simple linear growth along that dimension.
numbers: Pilot N = 75 children (grades 1, 3, 5), 4 weekly probability questions; fit RMSEA .075, CFI .911, TLI .930 (below the usual .95).
quote: No substantive conclusions from this illustration can be drawn.
limits: Illustration only; one category almost empty; internal inconsistencies in study length; author's claim of successful use rests on one other study.
agent_relevance: Overlapping waves is a metaphor with thin formal tests. Do not design the agent around a claimed rise and fall of strategies.

source: Luwel, Verschaffel (2008) Analysing strategy use in terms of the four parameters of strategic competence (numerosity judgement)
finding: Applies Lemaire and Siegler's four parameters (repertoire, frequency, efficiency, adaptivity) with the choice/no-choice method. Adaptivity (matching strategy to item) improves with age and intelligence and is trainable by strategy feedback, more than by outcome feedback.
numbers: Study 1: all sixth graders and adults used both strategies, only 60 percent of third graders (40 percent used only the slow addition strategy). Subtraction use 12 percent (grade 3), 33 percent (grade 6), 36 percent (adults). Study 2: 120 pupils (40 each low IQ about 77, average about 104, high about 129). Adaptivity gap to optimal switch point at pretest: low 10.49, average 10.25, high 5.18; at posttest 4.79, 5.23, 3.50. Strategy feedback beat outcome feedback: posttest gap 2.87 vs 6.17; subtraction use 61 vs 45 percent. Feedback had no effect for high-IQ children.
limits: One task (counting blocks in a grid), small groups, Greek pupils, secondary report of own earlier studies.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice improves when feedback names the strategy fit, not just right/wrong. For the agent: a failed check should say which method class failed, not only that the answer is wrong (G2).

source: Lemaire, Siegler (1995) Four aspects of strategic change; Siegler, Lemaire (1997) choice/no-choice method
finding: Children's multiplication shows several strategies at once; learning changes repertoire, frequency, speed/accuracy and adaptivity. The choice/no-choice method gives unbiased strategy efficiency, because in free choice people pick strategies on the items they suit.
numbers: Not read. Secondary description only (search summaries and Luwel and Verschaffel 2008).
limits: Original paper not opened. A 2012 multiplication study of 98 children is cited as confirming overlapping waves with latent growth models (summary only).
agent_relevance: Efficiency of a strategy must be measured without selection bias: run each method on the same items. Applies to benchmarking operators (compare arms on identical items).

source: Gick, Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Analogies help only when noticed or prompted. Spontaneous use is rare; a hint raises it a lot. Comparing two analogs builds a schema that predicts transfer.
numbers: Duncker radiation problem. About 10 percent solve with no analog; about 75 percent with an analog and a hint; only about 30 percent without a hint (so a third or less of those able to apply the analogy noticed it). Two analogs vs one: 45 vs 21 percent before hint; 80 vs 53 total. Pendulum problem: 71 vs 20 percent before hint, 98 vs 30 total. Schema quality: 94 percent of good-schema writers solved the target vs 53 percent of poor-schema writers (with-principle group); 86 vs 57 percent in the without-principle group. Diagrams added to two analogs: 92 percent total.
limits: Student volunteers, one target problem family; base rate of 10 percent borrowed from other studies rather than run in each experiment; no true no-analog control in several experiments.
agent_relevance: The gap between having an analogy and using it is the central finding. The agent needs an explicit retrieval step for relevant solved cases (and a check that the analogy maps), not hope that it notices.

source: Catrambone, Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Boundary conditions on analogical transfer. Transfer without a hint appeared when analogs and target were in one session and comparison was explicit; it fell to the baseline after a context shift or a delay; it came back (about 74 percent overall after a one-week delay) only with three analogs, schema-focused questions and a target reworded to stress the shared structure.
numbers: Five experiments. Baseline without analog 10 percent. After context shift with 30-minute vs 1-week delay: total solutions 65 vs 42 percent, before hint none above baseline. Two analogs vs one plus control: 71 vs 41 percent total. One-analog groups without comparison: 25 vs 30 percent before and after hint. Experiment 5: 74 percent produced the solution overall.
limits: Small groups (cells of 7 to 33), college students, one target problem.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of past solutions fails across context and time unless abstracted; store abstracted schemas, not raw traces (relevant to Soar-style learning notes, not covered here).

source: Seiter, Krabbe (2025) Analoges Problemloesen auf dem Pruefstand: Reproduzierbarkeit und neue Erkenntnisse (replication of Gick and Holyoak 1980 and Holyoak and Koh 1987)
finding: A conceptual replication with school pupils found no clear effect of the strategy shown in the source story on the strategy used for the target; only transfer distance (closer source, stronger effect) held up. The authors suggest person traits matter.
numbers: Tumour target: N = 282 pupils; group by strategy chi-square(15) = 22.10, p = .105, Cramer's V = .13 (all codings). Energy-supply target N = 190. With the tumour problem unnamed (N = 195): chi-square(15) = 25.42, p < .05, V = .16, small. Control group alone gave the splitting solution 51 percent of the time; bulb story group 88 percent, laser 73 percent, conquest 47 to 57 percent (nearer sources gave more). Coder agreement kappa .83. An earlier try (Seiter and Krabbe 2024; 40 adults, 37 pupils) also failed to confirm.
limits: Conference paper, German, different materials and strategy coding than the 1980 study; adolescents instead of psychology students; control rate far above the 10 percent base rate in the original (differences in what counted as a solution).
agent_relevance: Classic analogy-transfer effects are weaker and less general than textbooks say. Plan for analogy as a low-yield operator unless a check shows it helped.

source: Sinha, Kapur (2021) When problem solving followed by instruction works: Evidence for productive failure
finding: Meta-analysis on whether trying to solve a problem before being taught the method beats being taught first. Authors report an advantage for problem-solving-first when design fidelity is high.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons (per search summary and press write-ups). Pooled effect size not obtained; Kapur's own press claims, not the paper's table, speak of large effects at high fidelity.
limits: Not opened; effect sizes unverified. Authors are the proponents of the idea; school and university mathematics and science, not general reasoning.
agent_relevance: Support for letting the agent attempt first and learn from the failed attempt (G2 reading of real output), but only if the effect size is confirmed. Open item for the next pass.

source: Greiff, Wuestenberg et al. line of work, summarized in Molnar and Csapo (2018) and Wu and Molnar (2022): VOTAT and CPS
finding: Many studies find VOTAT users acquire more structure knowledge than others; however, the same literature reports strong confounding with reasoning ability and counter-examples where effective strategies did not give high control scores.
numbers: Cited: Fischer et al. (2012) VOTAT best for identifying causal relations; Vollmeyer et al. (1996) and Kroener et al. (2005) more structural knowledge for systematic explorers. In Schoppek and Fischer (2017) correlation between structural knowledge and control performance only about r = .35 to .41, with many cases that do not follow the trend.
limits: Second-hand citations as quoted inside two opened papers; original studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Knowing the structure of a problem and acting well on it are partly separate. The agent should not treat a correct model of the problem as proof of a correct plan.

source: Schoppek, Fischer (2017), knowledge and performance dissociation
finding: Structural knowledge and control performance correlate only moderately; some people controlled the system well with poor knowledge and others the reverse. PULSE use is tied to knowledge and performance more in MicroDYN than in Dynamis2.
numbers: Aggregated over three problems r = .35 (PULSE with knowledge) to r = .41 (knowledge with performance); partial correlations .35 and .39 with controls. PULSE-performance r = .401 vs .344 after controlling VOTAT in Dynamis2; PULSE-knowledge r = .524 (MicroDYN) vs .330 (Dynamis2). The authors call this 'not convincing evidence for an essential function of complete structural knowledge'.
limits: Single study, N = 165 with partial designs per cell, exploratory analyses flagged by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping separate checks for the model of the problem and for the outcome (G3); a good explanation is not proof of a good action.

source: Molnar, Csapo (2018), complexity and age moderators
finding: Strategy effectiveness depends on problem complexity and learner age, so the same strategy label gives very different success rates.
numbers: Effective-strategy use fell by about 20 percent as input variables increased and rose about 20 percent per age cohort. In grades 3 to 5 on the easiest problems effective strategies were used by 58.2 percent (80.1 percent of those scored high); for the most complex problems in grades 8 to 12 effective use was also 58 percent but only 60 percent of them solved it, against over 80 percent in the easy case. The +1+2 sequence worked on low-complexity problems but gave good solutions with low probability on complex ones.
limits: Cohorts are cross-sectional and the complexity levels differ in the number of variables only.
agent_relevance: A strategy that works on small problems degrades on larger ones. The router should include size/difficulty signals and re-check when a problem grows.

source: Wu, Molnar (2022), strategy by reasoning moderators
finding: Reasoning ability's link to success differs by strategy profile; the groups with weak strategy use show larger shortfalls that reasoning does not close.
numbers: CPS means by profile 61.37, 35.39, 27.03, 22.75 percent; knowledge acquisition: inductive reasoning predicted only in proficient (beta .363) and rapid learners (.327); knowledge application: inductive reasoning beta .339 to .447 in all groups; combinatorial reasoning predicted none. Reliability: CPS alpha .89, inductive .87, combinatorial .79.
limits: Correlational; the claim that reasoning must be trained first is not shown by the data.
agent_relevance: Between-person strategy gaps are large (up to about 38 points) so a scaffold that enforces good exploration has a real target even if reasoning is held fixed.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover, ablation and error analysis
finding: Selecting modules is not enough: the SELECT, ADAPT and IMPLEMENT steps each add accuracy, and task-specific adaptation matters. Errors after a correct structure are mostly arithmetic.
numbers: 87.5 percent (175 of 200) MATH structures correct; 74.7 percent of failures from computation errors; wrong structures only 25.3 percent of errors. On 4 tasks with GPT-4 the authors report that applying all three actions (select, adapt, implement) works best.
limits: Ablation on 4 tasks and GPT-4 only; error audit by the authors on 200 items.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice is rarely the bottleneck on math; execution is. Pair strategy selection with code-run arithmetic and checks (G2, G3).

source: Gunasekara, Ratnayake (2025), few-shot and granularity moderators
finding: Whether extra examples or per-instance planning help depends on how uniform the benchmark is: they help on coherent tasks (T4D) and not on diverse ones (BBH).
numbers: T4D unstructured: 5-shot 86.35 (LLaMA) and 88.29 (Mistral) vs 0-shot 78.90 and 82.09. BBH unstructured: LLaMA 87.02 (5-shot) vs 87.27 (0-shot), Mistral 86.29 vs 85.57. Instance-level beat task-level on BBH by 4.30 points (Mistral) and 0.79 (LLaMA), while task-level won on T4D (100.00 vs 78.90 for LLaMA).
limits: Two small open models; accuracy 100 percent for task-level on T4D suggests a ceiling effect.
agent_relevance: For batches of similar items, a shared plan with a few worked cases is efficient; for mixed items, plan per item. Matches a gate at S0.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Adaptive-Solver, component contributions
finding: More samples alone do not buy accuracy cost-efficiently; benefits plateau and in some settings fall. Escalating by problem difficulty works better.
numbers: Self-consistency accuracy plateaus with sample size and drops in some cases (GPT-3.5 CoT and least-to-most on MAWPS). GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 gap about 6 to 16 points at 7 to 13 times the cost. Four adaptation types: model, sample size, prompt method, decomposition granularity.
limits: Data from the arXiv v2 text only; cost numbers depend on 2023 API prices.
agent_relevance: Use sampling as a signal (disagreement triggers escalation), not as a default output rule (G4, G5).

source: Luwel, Verschaffel (2008), context moderator
finding: Task context changes strategy frequency: when the grid size varied from trial to trial (mixed condition) adults used the efficient subtraction strategy less than when it was constant, because it needs an extra step each time.
numbers: Subtraction strategy on 47 percent of trials in the pure condition vs 38 percent in the mixed condition (adults, Study 3).
limits: Adults, one task; report is a secondary summary of the authors' own studies.
agent_relevance: Extra set-up cost makes a better method less likely to be chosen. Make the better operator cheap to invoke (one call, ready template) or it will be skipped.
